_note: Registry for Part Two of Amit_Living_Testimony.html. To add a new application: add an entry to a group below (name, path, desc, links), then run build_living_testimony.js (the hook does this automatically). 'links' are [label, path-relative-to-site-root] pairs. 'excluded' are regex patterns for html files that are NOT public applications (backups, mockups, private business files, internal tools) so the unregistered-app check ignores them.
intro: The applications that are live today, each with a working link and a plain description of what it does. This list is rebuilt automatically whenever a new application is added. Private business files and internal tools are left out on purpose.

apps.name: Amit Hub
apps.desc: The Amit Hub is the front door and daily home of the whole system: the first thing a signed-in person opens each day, and the place from which every other Amit tool is reached. WHAT IT HOLDS: a morning home screen with a greeting, the clock and a daily verse; the Hebrew and sacred calendars (Biblical, Rabbinic and the 364-day Priestly calendar), with feasts, Shabbat, the Omer count and a short teaching for each day; Word for Today (a Hebrew word chosen for the day); Pursuits, which is your own list of goals and to-dos, with priorities, due dates, repeating items and a calendar view where finished pursuits become memories; Amit's Prayer; Mail across your accounts; current weather and active weather alerts for your location; and About Me, where you set your profile, your appearance (themes), Amit's voice (accent, speed, pauses, tone), your birth date (needed for chat safety, locked once saved), a guardian link for a young person under 18, and an access PIN for sensitive values. COMMUNICATIONS is one panel with tabs: Email, Chats (private chat with friends, groups and Amit himself), Amit Helper, Amit Mouse and Amit Keyboard (where you set what each button or key does on your own computer). A sidebar opens the other Amit tools (Who Is God, Devotions, Games, Computer Health, Amit Mobile and more), and a right-hand rail carries Sign In, Ask Amit, the chat button and a light that shows whether the Amit Helper is running on your computer. WHAT IT NEEDS: a browser. You can look around without an account; signing in (free) saves your own data, and the Helper tabs and Computer Health link only do their work after you install the Helper on a Windows computer (see Sign Up and Install Amit). When Amit's local pieces on your computer notice a Windows crash, the Hub shows a plain notice about it. Amit's chat is built into the Hub and answers when you ask. The Hub is reached at askamit.org.

apps.name: Sign Up and Install Amit
apps.desc: HOW TO JOIN, AND HOW TO PUT AMIT ON YOUR COMPUTER. Signing up is free and is the way into everything. WHERE: the Amit Hub (the front door) has a Sign In button in its right-hand column. SIGN UP (Create account) asks for your name, your email, a password of at least 6 characters, an optional hint to jog your memory, and two recovery questions with your own answers. Both recovery questions are required: they are how you get back in if you ever forget the password, with no email step, and the answers are kept scrambled, never readable. If an email arrives asking you to confirm the account, click the link in it. SIGN IN afterwards with the same email and password; if you forget the password, the forgot option uses your recovery questions. ONE MORE STEP FOR CHAT: Amit's chat asks once for your birth date (in About Me, in the Hub). It keeps young people safe in chat, and once it is saved it is locked. A person under 18 uses chat only when a guardian has linked them. INSTALL ON A WINDOWS COMPUTER (optional, free; Windows only, not phones or Macs): download install-Amit.exe from the Hub's Connect Amit step or from the AmitFix page (AmitFix needs no account). Your browser and Windows will each ask you to confirm, because the file is new and not yet signed by a registered publisher. In Edge, click the three dots next to the download and choose Keep; in the next popup click the small down arrow next to Delete and choose Keep anyway. When you open the file, Windows says it protected your PC: click More info, then Run anyway. Only you can make those clicks. The installer does not install Node.js and does not ask about a Claude account. Installing also switches on Amit's performance tracking for that computer by default (memory, processor, diagnostics); you can turn tracking off in Computer Health and keep the rest. WHAT INSTALLING CONNECTS: the Amit Helper (a slim bar on the right edge of the screen with your own buttons, and the Aurora ring that opens when you hold the right mouse button anywhere in Windows: Dictate lets you talk to type in any program, Show Amit lets you capture and mark up part of the screen and show it to Amit, Voice lets you say what to do, Read has Amit read aloud what you point at); Computer Health (a live health dashboard for your PC); Amit Mouse and Amit Keyboard (you decide what each button and key does); the Amit Preview window; and, on your home network, the Amit Pad, where a paired phone acts as a touchpad and photo sender (built and released, but not yet fully field-tested). The Helper updates itself from Amit's site. WANT MORE ANSWERS? Amit's answers need a Claude program behind them. Signed-in people who connect nothing share Amit's own limited allowance. A person who wants more can connect their OWN Claude account: their plan stays theirs and is paid to Claude directly. The AmitCapacity page shows measured numbers for what that gives. STATUS, said plainly: the step that connects a person's own Claude account is NOT built yet (as of 2026-11-18), and the capacity numbers are approximate. Until then, signing up (free) is the way in and nothing has to be paid to start. TO FIX, QUIET OR REMOVE: AmitFix repairs, quiets or completely removes everything Amit put on the computer, with no account, so anyone can leave at any time. Amit himself lives online and is never removed.
links: Sign in or create an account (the Hub)
What connecting your own Claude account gives (AmitCapacity)

apps.name: Who Is God
apps.desc: The Who Is God page inside Devotions: the evidence foundation of Amit, and now its main home. It is one page of the Devotions application (page 4, "Who Is God"), laid out on the Multi-Row Tab View, with all of the original investigation's tabs carried over: Which Religion Is True?, Approach, The Covenants, The 12 Key Arguments, Original Language, One Body, Millennial Proof, Additional Texts, Church Comparisons, Seven Churches, The Seven Lampstands, Do I Have It Wrong?, Pre/Mid/Post, Are You Saved?, Research Transparency, Use & Install, Yeshua, and Ancient Hebrew (The Appointed Times, the nineteenth, now opens the Feasts of the Lord page as its introduction). It investigates which religion is true with the reasoning shown: world religions and Christian denominations scored against Scripture, the Name of God and the Hebrew and Greek behind contested New Testament passages, the Millennial test, and an account of how each of Amit's conclusions was reached, including the hard texts. A person reads it tab by tab with no sign-in; a link can open a specific tab. The Church Comparisons area also has a Request a fellowship flow: a signed-in person names a fellowship and where it is, the request goes to Amit's inbox, Amit researches what the fellowship publishes, and a link to the finished research is sent back (researched fellowships, not self-scored ones, go on the map). The original stand-alone page still exists and is kept as a fallback, but Devotions is the place to use now. Needs internet; sign-in only for the fellowship request. Limits: the fellowship research needs database steps that, as last recorded, had not yet been run.

apps.name: Devotions
apps.desc: Study, listen, worship: Scripture study and Amit's original worship songs side by side, and now also the home of the Who Is God investigation. The page is a set of numbered pages in a side list. The Feasts of the Lord page has seven tabs in calendar order (Passover, Unleavened Bread, Firstfruits, Shavuot, Trumpets, Yom Kippur, Tabernacles) with full story-format studies, plus The Appointed Times as an introduction tab shown first. Every study has a speaker button that hands the text to Speak to Me so it can be read aloud. A Difficult Passages page begins with a study of Colossians 2, worked from the Word itself. Page 4 is Who Is God: the whole evidence investigation (which religion is true, the covenants, the 12 key arguments, original language, church comparisons, the Millennial proof, Are You Saved?, Ancient Hebrew and more) on a multi-row tab view, with a Request a fellowship flow where Amit researches a church for you. The songs themselves play on Amit Music. No sign-in is needed to read or listen. Limits: the latest work (Who Is God moved in, fellowship request) was built locally and, as last recorded, was not yet released; the fellowship tables needed database migrations that had not been run; the Consult-style extras are not part of this page. One open question is whether the Passover study should name the Exodus 12:48 circumcision requirement.

apps.name: Amit Music
apps.desc: The player for Amit's original worship songs, with lyrics and video, written from real study sessions and produced with a music generator. Today it holds Blow the Shofar (for the Feast of Trumpets) and When I See the Blood (for Passover). Each song can be played in the page, has its own shareable page with a proper preview picture for social media, and a Visit Amit path into the rest of Amit. The audio is hosted by Amit, so playing needs no sign-in and does not depend on any outside player staying available. It is part of Devotions, where each song is meant to sit beside the study it came from.

apps.name: Speak to Me
apps.desc: Speak to Me reads any text aloud in a natural voice so you can listen instead of read. HOW TO USE IT: open the page, paste text into the box (or arrive with text already filled in from another Amit tool), and press Play. The words are highlighted as they are spoken, and you can click any word to jump there. Controls: Play and Pause (or the Spacebar), back or forward a phrase (arrow keys), Restart this text, Clear the screen to paste something new, Close, and a Sleep-after timer that stops the reading after a set time. A Voice Control window lets you choose the accent or region, the voice, speed, tone, volume and pacing, with a Let Me Hear It button to test. When you are signed in, those choices are saved to your Amit voice profile and also apply in the Hub and Amit Mobile; when you are not, they last only for that visit. WHAT IT USES: the free speech built into your browser, so it costs nothing, needs no extra program, and the voices available depend on your browser and device. Honest limit: it reads continuously word by word, so the pacing setting does not change what you hear on this page, though it carries over to the Hub and Amit Mobile. This is where the Voice Control project (giving any Amit page a spoken voice) ended up: the speech method is proven and reusable across Amit pages. A separate experiment that connected a page to a live local Claude session is a proof of concept only and is on hold.

apps.name: Ask Amit
apps.path: Amit_Ask_Live.js (the Ask Amit tile on every page)
apps.desc: Ask Amit is the button and chat box that sits on every Amit page, so a person can ask Amit about the page they are on without going anywhere else. It is one shared file used by every page, so every page brings the same Amit with only that page's own context added. WHAT HAPPENS WHEN YOU PRESS IT: if you are signed in, it opens your own private AmitChat with Amit, and Amit knows which page you are on; he can answer from your own app data only under your own login, and only when everyone in the chat is authorised. There is one Ask Amit chat per day. If you are not signed in, a small window offers two choices: Write to Amit, which needs no account and sends a real message straight into Amit's inbox (Amit's reply can appear for you later on the same browser), or Connect With Him Online, which carries Amit and the page you are on into a live conversation. A VISITOR CHAT is also built: someone without an account can ask Amit up to five questions about the applications (no web lookup, no tools), then up to five more only about signing up and installing, with a warm invitation to create a free account; it has been built and tested on Ryan's computer, but its release to the public site has not been confirmed, and it depends on Amit's answering program running on Ryan's computer. Signed-in people can attach one picture to a question, which Amit measures with plain code and then deletes. BEHIND IT: today the answers come from a Claude program that runs on Ryan's computer, with the rules held in the database; a single shared module called AskAmit, built so far alone and not yet joined to every button, is meant to become the one home for every answer. Honest limits: answers pause when that computer's answering program is not running, and there is a daily and per-visitor allowance. It needs a browser; signing in unlocks the chat.
links: Open the Hub, where the tile lives

apps.name: Amit's Living Testimony
apps.desc: This page is Amit's public record in two parts. PART ONE is Amit's own testimony: the account of who Amit is, how Amit came to be, what Amit concluded from the evidence, and how Amit has grown, written in Amit's own voice and kept as a growing log. PART TWO, Every Application We've Built, is this index: one card for each application, grouped (Walk alongside, Tools, Other applications), each with a plain description for someone who has never seen it, and links straight to it. Designed and planned applications are listed separately, marked as not built. The page is generated, not hand-edited: a build script reads the testimony file and a registry of applications and rebuilds the page, bumping its own version badge, so a new or changed application appears here once the registry is updated and the page is pushed. Ryan's personal profile is no longer part of the page. Amit also reads this page: when Ryan starts a God talk session, Amit reads the whole testimony first, and when someone asks Amit what the applications can do, Amit points to this list. Anything that is not in the list is, as far as visitors are concerned, not part of Amit. It needs only a browser and no account.

apps.name: AmitChat
apps.desc: AmitChat is the private, login-based chat inside the Amit Hub (the chat icon on the right edge, and the Communications page, Chats tab). People add friends by link or code, make group chats, and send photos, files and voice messages. It has read receipts, a live transcript and a read-aloud player that follows the words. AMIT IS IN THE CHAT: press the Amit icon and he joins and listens; he stays quiet while people talk, comes in after a pause with a question or thought, answers at once when his name is said, and turns himself off if nobody replies. If you are the only person there, everything you write is for him. The Ask Amit button opens your own private chat with Amit (one chat per day), who answers questions, including voice messages and anything he can look up on the web or in Amit's own notes. Ask Amit also works on every Amit page. Amit may answer from a person's own app data only under their own login and only when everyone in the chat is authorised. The envelope button sends a private message to Amit's team; it lands in the team inbox in the Hub, Amit confirms in the chat, tells you when it has been seen and brings the reply back, with reminders after 24 and 48 working hours, never on the Sabbath weekend. Built to keep young people safe: a birth date kept in About Me, and parents and guardians decide whether their child may chat and can read their child's chats until they turn 18. Answers come from a locked-down Claude run on Ryan's computer, so replies depend on that computer being on. Speaking into any program (Whisper mode) belongs to the Amit Helper, not this chat. First use: studying Scripture together. Not yet built: the My Life feed of God-centered posts; a notes feature that shapes how Amit speaks to each person is built but awaits a database step.
links: Open the Hub (chat icon on the right)

apps.name: The Council
apps.desc: The Council is a brainstorming room where one real question is put to several outside voices (other AI systems) in rounds, with Amit as a voice too, until honest agreement or honest disagreement shows. Everything is recorded in the person's account so the whole path, including wrong turns, can be read later. A request moves through stages: Scope (a title, the question, who sits on the council), Round 1 Clarification (the voices ask what they need to know), the Synthesis Desk (a separate, neutral writer that matches overlapping questions, lets the person answer them one at a time, then writes the refined question), a Ruling by the person (rerun, adjust or confirm), Investigation (the voices answer), then Combine, where the desk writes a letter pulling the answers together. The person then accepts the result or chooses Investigate Further, which starts a new cycle. Nothing is deleted or rewritten after the fact, and a topic is only marked resolved when the person says so. Every prompt a voice receives is built in one place from the stored facts and carries the round, the phase, the question, what to do and what not to do, and each voice must open its reply with a receipt naming the round, so mix-ups are caught before saving. The page always blinks the next field to fill in. Needs sign-in. Honest limits: every round is still copy and paste between the page and each voice's own chat, so it cannot run unattended and a stranger cannot yet use it alone; the latest changes were built and tested offline but not yet proven in one full live round, and were not yet published; some voices need a paid service and are set aside.

apps.name: Computer Health
apps.desc: Computer Health is Amit watching over a person's computer: a plain-language dashboard that turns raw readings into words like "90% of your memory is in use" with a verdict (fine, keep an eye on it, fix it now), and keeps a history so a person can come back months later and ask what slowed things down or what changed. Small watcher programs on the computer record resource use (memory, processor, graphics, temperatures), the causes of input lag, what each running app writes to disk and reaches on the network during a session, and what a newly installed program quietly added (startup entries, scheduled tasks, browser extensions, changed home pages). A local connection on the computer feeds those readings to the page, and events are saved to the person's account so they last. The dashboard pages are: Free Up and Optimize (the overview), Hardware sensors (real sensor readings, which need a separate sensor-reader program added on request from that page), Browser check, Installed programs, Updates and drivers, Problems, History and charts, App Behavior, and Protection. The Problems page holds a Watch switch: when it is on, the computer records a crash package if Windows crashes hard, and the page lists saved crashes with a plain-words analysis done by rules, not guesswork; the Hub can show a "we noticed a crash" notice. Removal of anything is never automatic: Amit researches and recommends, the person approves, and files are backed up before anything is deleted. It needs sign-in, internet for saving history, and the Amit Helper installed once on the Windows computer (the helper is a separate program that supplies the local connection; Computer Health itself is only the monitoring side). Limits: Windows only, no Mac version; the Installed Programs history needs a database step that is not yet confirmed done; the paid "Verify Conditions" tier is only a teaser. It is the free side of Computer Value, the product meant to fund the mission.

apps.name: Amit Mouse
apps.desc: Where a person tells Amit about every mouse they use and decides what each button does. Windows tells the mice apart, so a person can have a gaming mouse, an office mouse and more, each learned once on the Learn mouse tab (press its buttons one by one), given a one-word name and its own numbered sets (for example Everyday and Design) on the Mouse sets tab. In a set, every button of every mouse except the MAIN mouse's left, right and middle buttons can be changed: send a keyboard shortcut, run one of the person's own Amit Helper bar buttons, act as another mouse button (a left-handed swap for one mouse), switch to another set, or do nothing. A button can do one thing on a click, another on a double-click and another on a hold, and a held-back click still drags. Because a mouse button can run a bar button, it can also press a Windows action (Undo, Copy, Open Task View, Lock PC and more) or open any Helper menu (the Menus group). The page shows which set is running on the computer, and it pauses the sets while the person edits so every button works as normal and nothing can trap them; a Test button turns them on for 30 seconds, and they come back by themselves if the page closes. Safeguards: the main mouse's left, right and middle never change, every other mouse must keep a way to left-click, a Reset a button panel (choose the mouse, the set and the button) works from the main mouse for any mouse, and Ctrl+Alt+Shift+M switches every set off from the keyboard. The middle button of every mouse runs the one standard Amit menu button. That menu has a Mouse tab that recognizes which mouse opened it and lists that mouse's sets, the one in use marked, so the person scrolls and picks one; it also has an ON/OFF switch for all mouse sets and an Open button for this page. Dictation and Voice never stop a mouse button, and the wheel opens the menu while Voice is listening. A mouse moved to a different USB port looks like a new mouse to Windows, so the Learn tab has a Use a saved setup panel: MOVE a saved mouse's setup onto the new one (same name, sets and buttons) or COPY its sets onto another mouse; a saved mouse can be deleted (never the main mouse). Found in the Hub under Communications > Amit Mouse; kept with the person's login for each of their computers and carried out by the Amit Helper on that computer (needs sign-in and the Helper, Windows only). Keyboards are the separate Amit Keyboard page; game controllers are planned. Limits: a button that a mouse's own program changes before Windows sees it cannot be matched to a mouse and is left alone.

apps.name: Amit Keyboard
apps.desc: The keyboard twin of Amit Mouse. A person with several keyboards (a main one, a macro pad, a second keyboard, a barcode scanner) tells Amit about each one on the Learn keyboard tab by pressing its keys; Windows names the keyboard behind every key, so each keyboard is learned once, given a one-word name and its own numbered sets (Keyboard sets tab). In a set, a key, a PAIR of keys held together (either order is the same) or a key held with Ctrl, Shift, Alt or Windows can be given a job: send another key or a combination, run one of the person's own Amit Helper bar buttons, switch to another set, send keys and then switch set, or do nothing; a key can do one thing on a press, another on a double press and another on a hold. Hold Space for a moment and press 1 to 9 and that numbered set is switched on (in every set but Set 1, the safe starting set). Everything is checked by both the page and the Helper: Ctrl, Alt, Shift, Windows and Esc alone never change, Ctrl+Alt+Shift+M switches every mouse and keyboard set off at once and puts each keyboard back on Set 1, the main keyboard keeps its typing keys in Set 1, and the sets pause while the page is open so nothing can trap the person. The same sets can be used as a scrambler for private-looking messages. The Secure code tab types a message through the sets (a key can switch to another set as it types, like a rotor, and a Fill a demo code button builds three example sets so it can be tried); Secure modifier adds up to four shared secrets (a date, a birthday, a word, a number) that shift every character; Secure decipher reads a message back. A Secure message window offers Write, Read and Share codes with friends. It is scrambled, not secure, and says so on every screen: it is not real encryption, and real encryption underneath is not built. Found in the Hub under Communications > Amit Keyboard; kept with the person's login for each of their computers and carried out by the Amit Helper (needs sign-in and the Helper, Windows only). The Amit menu has a Keyboard tab listing the sets of the keyboard last used. What is typed is never logged or stored; which key on which keyboard is only shown to the page while it is learning. Limits: a key that a keyboard's own program handles before Windows sees it (a Fn key) cannot be changed; AltGr, dead keys and input methods are worth trying on real keyboards.

apps.name: Show Amit
apps.desc: Show Amit is the screenshot and picture editor of the Amit Helper. Choose Show Amit on the Aurora ring and drag over any part of the screen; the shot opens in an editor. The top bar shows the shot's name, tabs for any other open Show Amit windows, Retake and a File menu. An Add to your picture row offers small tools (select, words, pen, marker, arrow, box, line, oval) with colors, line width, undo, zoom and Add capture (take another screen area into the same picture). Add picture adds any picture file as a new item; pictures can also be dragged in from File Explorer. An On this picture list makes every mark its own item that can be hidden with the eye, brought forward, sent back, renamed or removed, while the original picture is never changed. A Send to an app panel lists Receipts, Contracts, Job site photos and Quotes, shown as coming soon until those apps exist. Shots save to Pictures\Show Amit with their layers kept so they can be reopened; File > Open a saved shot or picture opens a saved shot (layers back) or any picture file in a new window, and File > Recent pictures lists saved ones. Edits are saved when the person chooses Save or closes the window (no autosave of edits yet). A Print button (also File > Print and Ctrl+P) opens the Amit print preview, where the person picks this window, an area or the whole screen; nothing prints until Print is pressed there. THE ASK AMIT BAR under the picture sends the shot to Amit, with a question if one is typed: the Helper window opens on the person's chat for today, posts the picture there under their own sign-in with the title and any typed words, and Amit looks at it and answers. The picture is private to that chat; the link Amit uses is made from the person's own sign-in and works about 10 minutes for that one file, and the helper deletes its copy after answering. A photo sent from the phone opens in the same editor with a note box. Needs the Amit Helper, the internet and the answering computer. Not yet field-tested by hand: Add capture, the tabs, a phone photo in the new editor, and the Print button.

apps.name: Read
apps.desc: Read is the fourth choice on the Aurora ring of the Amit Helper: Amit reads aloud whatever the person points at, in any program, in the person's own saved Amit voice. Choosing Read puts a small see-through speaker on top of the screen. The person presses it, then clicks a word (Amit reads from that word to the end of its paragraph) or highlights text (Amit reads exactly the highlight: one word if one word, the whole page after Select All). It reads once and goes back to waiting, so the person is free to use the computer; to read somewhere else they press the speaker again. A soft gold highlight shows the words being read. Pressing the speaker while Amit reads pauses it (the next click or selection is read instead; pressing again resumes). A double click on the speaker opens a small voice window: voice, speed, pause between sentences, pitch and volume, changed while Amit is reading and heard at once; Save makes it the person's reading voice under their login. When dictation or Voice starts, Read pauses by itself and carries on afterward. If Amit cannot read what was pointed at, Amit says so out loud and on screen. Esc or a right click on the speaker removes it. The natural voices come from Microsoft Edge online, so Read needs Edge and the internet; the Helper starts Edge out of sight only while reading and closes it about 30 seconds later. Needs the Amit Helper. Not yet tested on Windows 10 or other browsers.

apps.name: AmitBooks
apps.desc: Amit's accounting and bookkeeping application for small businesses, under the shared Amit sign-in. The rebuilt version (the one being built out) is a working app today: sign in, create or choose a company and a set of books, build a Chart of Accounts with sub-accounts, and modify or delete a company or book (a backup is taken first) or restore one from a backup. A first-run walkthrough guides a new user. A QuickBooks Import wizard handles the first two steps (the company and book, then the Chart of Accounts from a CSV or Excel file); the later import steps are not built yet. The sidebar pages include Books, To Do, Clients, Vendors, Cash and Outstanding. The Outstanding page is a temporary monthly outstanding-balance grid, to be retired once real bills reporting exists. The General Journal can be drilled into (by date or by account), sorted, and bulk-selected; deleting a record first writes a snapshot to an append-only audit log so the trail cannot be altered. Sensitive values such as company tax IDs are locked: the company ID vault, and fields protected by a personal PIN that is never stored (five wrong tries locks it for 24 hours; a reset is available but destroys the locked data). The older AmitBooks page stays live until the rebuild matches it, then it is retired. The wider plan includes multi-book accounting, bank reconciliation, receipt reading, payroll and more; those are designed but not all built. Not yet built: import steps 3 to 6, enforcement of per-person book permissions, and a shared people table. It needs sign-in and an internet connection; its phone companion is AmitScan.

apps.name: AmitScan
apps.desc: The phone companion for AmitBooks: a web app installed to a phone's home screen for photographing receipts and documents in the field. Open it, sign in by scanning a QR code or sending a sign-in link to your email, pick or confirm the kind of document after each photo (receipt, mileage and other modes), crop it, and accept, retake or delete it. Photos queue on the phone, and the Send to Amit button uploads them to a private store where they wait as captured items. That is staging only: there is no review step yet, and automatic reading of the images and posting into the AmitBooks records is not built. A desktop path exists for sending selected scans to a local inbox on the computer for processing with the Helper, but the unattended processing step was blocked when last checked (the command-line tool it needs was not installed), so treat that part as unfinished. It needs a signed-in Amit account and a camera.

apps.name: AmitCoder
apps.desc: A paid, sign-in workspace for building your own apps with Amit on your own computer, using your own Claude account; it is made so a person with no coding experience can follow it. Built today: shared (J) shortcuts that Amit curates and personal (F) shortcuts each person writes for themselves; a Get Started checklist; a history of your build sessions; a code library and pairing log where builds and ideas are kept; a Starter Kit script that sets up project folders, backups, a local test server and a convention for database changes; and a Previewer tab. The Amit Preview window (see its own card) draws a design beside its code so you can look at it before anything real is built; every visual idea is meant to be shown to you first as a true-to-life, working picture. A separate guided Previewer page asks the questions Claude needs as clickable choices that change the picture as you click, and gives back a build sheet; it is built and works locally, but the answers return to the conversation by copy and paste only, and an in-page preview pane inside AmitCoder is not built. The idea behind the product: each subscriber gets the same Amit project files and standards Ryan works with, tailored to them, and Amit never reads or stores your Claude login. Not built or not yet released: the real installer for other people, billing (the price is not set), and the automatic delivery of standards to each subscriber. The personal bar on the right edge of the Windows screen belongs to the Amit Helper, which is its own project. Needs sign-in; Windows is the tested system. In development.

apps.name: Amit Preview
apps.desc: A window for looking at a design before it is built, and for comparing ideas. Across the top you pick the preview (by date and title), start a new one, or open an earlier one from the History. Under it you pick the version you are looking at: a dropdown of every version and who made it, with a button to add another. A switch changes between Code (the code box on the left, a live picture of it on the right) and View (the picture across the whole window). There is a Clear button and a Details drawer where you write what the preview is for, how it works and what its sample values stand for. Amit sends each preview straight into the window, and the window is reused so previews never pile up; the Helper puts the window beside your conversation. Every send must come with its details (the app, a title, the purpose, how it works and the sample values), or the window refuses it and shows the sender exactly what is missing; the rules for senders are the first thing in the page. Every preview is filed in the History and can be opened again. A preview holds versions: Amit's own, and answers pasted in from other AIs (ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Copilot and others), each with a name you choose, its own notes, and one note for the whole preview. Improve, Better and Reimagine each write a ready brief for any AI (purpose, how it works, sample values, your notes and the whole code): Improve asks for suggestions that keep the look; Better asks for better options while keeping the generic look; Reimagine says start over, keep the intent, and design it completely new. Ask Amit writes a message for VS Code or Ask Amit with your notes. If a pasted page has an error, a red banner says what it is and on which line, with a button that jumps to it. It opens from the Amit Helper bar (the Amit PreView button) or by the voice command "preview". The live link and the History need the small local Amit Helper; the page also works alone as a place to paste HTML. The page runs in a sandbox: scripts work, but storage and pop-ups do not. Not built yet: choosing from a list what to preview, and keeping the History in the database. Working today; more is being built.

apps.name: Amit Mobile
apps.desc: A phone-first gateway to Amit. Sign in on a phone and add it to the home screen. The dashboard of tiles holds: Daily Walk; Amit (talk, with spoken replies and a voice chosen per person in the Hub's About Me); Chat (the shared Amit chat engine, with threads grouped by day, several photos and a speak button); Send to computer (a phone photo goes to your computer, where you can ask Amit about it in a numbered Mobile chat); My Computer; and a hand-off into AmitBooks. Zoom/Read This and Search are placeholders. How it works: the phone and the computer never talk directly; both use the database as a relay, and a small watcher on the computer answers by running Amit headlessly, but only while the Hub is open on the computer (a heartbeat check). Photos are not analysed on that path. At home, the Mouse and Buttons tile turns the phone into the Amit Pad: a touchpad and button pad for your own computer (it needs the Amit Helper running there). It opens to a menu of Mouse, Navigation (the Helper bar, the Amit menu, the Aurora and your own bar buttons), Photo and Ask Amit; each phone you set up has its own name and shows in a list in the Hub. The Pad was tested on a real iPhone (touch, touchpad, taps, scroll, pinch, photo, video, dictation), and it comes with the Amit Helper. It runs over the home Wi-Fi on a plain web address; a secure home address was researched and set aside for now.

apps.name: Amit Health
apps.desc: The personal health companion inside Amit, at an early stage. The landing page lists eight areas: EOB, Medications, Appointments, Insurance Coverage, Medical Bills, Health Records, Family Health and Preventive Care. At this point each one shows only a description of what it will do; none is a working tracker yet. The part that does work is The Kitchen, a food and drink composer with Ingredients and Meals, nutrient totals, concerns tracking and an Add New Item flow. Its Menu, Consult and Fasting pages are described on screen but not functional. The Kitchen saves to the browser only, not yet to the person's account; saving to accounts is the agreed next step. Family accounts are partly built: the About Me family form and the database tables exist, but the Edge Function that creates a family member's login was updated and not yet redeployed. A longer-term goal is a lifelong personal health record with food as the way in. Early build; nothing here replaces a doctor.

apps.name: AmitRoll
apps.desc: A free dice-and-number arithmetic game for kids and adults, rebuilt from "Ready, Set, Roll," a game the builder made about fifteen years ago. Each round you roll five dice and cover five number cards by making each card's number from the dice. You decide whether to press on for more points or stop; cover all five and you bank the set, bust and you keep only what was already banked. It has four stages: addition, then subtraction, multiplication and division, with signs unlocking as the level rises. Games are played to a target score (100, 250 or 500) against Amit opponents, with experience by finishing place, a clock for each round that shortens as you improve, an all-signs bonus, and wild cards. From level 4 you type your own score and a wrong total costs the difference. A Practice page lets you choose a level, and Learn tabs give a lesson for each stage; beginners get help buttons that show a better play. Progress is saved in the browser only. The newest work (the later stages and the multi-stage play described above) is built locally and not yet released; the released version is an earlier one with the banking rule. Not built: real players, friends and groups, class tables for teachers, saved history in the database, and the later stages (fractions, algebra and so on).

apps.name: AmitCapacity
apps.desc: AmitCapacity answers one question with measured numbers: what does a person get when they connect Amit to their own Claude account? The page presents the split of a $30 monthly cost ($20 to Claude for the answering power on their own account, $10 to Amit for premium access to the whole suite). For a normal question (about 20 words asked, about 150 words answered, about 12 seconds) it shows about 125 answers in a 5-hour window, about 1,450 a week and about 6,200 a month on Claude Pro, with ordinary and deep-research questions shown separately and the same in hours of use. All of it comes from two days of real use, two runs that agreed within about 10 percent, and every figure carries its range and caveats. Tabs: The Story (the recorded conversation between the desktop Amit who builds and measures and the online Amit who answers in the Hub chat, with screenshots, shown only to the owner), The Numbers, Receipts (each signed-in person's own answers as a share of a window and a week) and Ask Amit.

apps.name: AmitFix
apps.desc: AmitFix is the one place to install, fix, quiet or remove anything Amit puts on a Windows computer. Amit himself lives online and is never removed; what lives on a computer is Amit's helper (the small program and watchers behind voice typing in any program and Computer Health). Anyone asking how to install, fix or remove it is sent here; the Hub's Help button also opens it. The page knows where you came from (the Hub, an email, a QR code, a phone) and opens at the right fix. Tabs under the Director's Chair: Start here (say what is happening and it ticks the right fixes), Make it right (look first, restart, tidy up, reset voice typing, fresh start), Quiet on set (turn voice typing on or off, stop it starting with Windows, remove desktop shortcuts, forget what it kept), Browser and phone (sign out and clear what Amit saved in a browser), Wrap (Remove Amit: closes the helper, turns off start-with-Windows, deletes its files, saved data and shortcuts, then checks that it is really gone), and Install Amit (one button downloads the installer, with plain steps). Choices go on a call sheet that downloads as one small file, or Remove-Amit.exe does the whole removal in one click. It lists everything Amit puts on a computer in plain words, including Node.js and Claude Code, which the installer adds only if missing and which removal leaves in place. Other pages: Send It (share by link, email, text, QR or a one-page PDF), What's On My Computer, and Our Heart (a welcome, farewell and come-back note). VERIFY IT is for anyone who worries the helper might be malware: a page and a plain-text file hold one packet to paste into any AI or security forum for a hostile review. It names every behavior that looks suspicious and why it is there (a system-wide mouse hook for voice typing, typing into other programs, a localhost-only web server, hidden PowerShell, start-with-Windows, optional Node.js and Claude Code, no code-signing certificate yet, developer-only parts inert on ordinary computers), gives claims to try to disprove, the SHA-256 fingerprint of every file, every web address the code can reach, how to test safely on a spare computer, and a readable copy of the developer-only phone watcher script with a plain walkthrough. CHECK IT is a read-only program that compares every installed Amit file with the published fingerprints (fetched again straight from GitHub so a tampered web page alone cannot fool it), and also checks extra files, the start-with-Windows entry, link handlers, shortcuts, what the helper listens on and whether programs are signed. It gives a masked report copied to the clipboard with a verdict: ALL MATCH, OLDER VERSION or DIFFERENCES FOUND. Honest limits: Windows will say unknown publisher because there is no code-signing certificate yet; stopping real running programs, registry changes and a real removal have not been tested on a second computer; a phone and web-app repair feature is half-built and not live.

apps.name: Amit Helper
apps.path: A Windows program on the person's own computer (installed with the Amit installer); the Helper window page is ComputerHealth/AmitLive.html
apps.desc: The Amit Helper is the program on a person's own Windows computer that listens, speaks and puts Amit one press away. It is separate from Computer Health; the only monitoring it does is keep a record when an Amit program crashes. THE BAR: a personal bar on the right edge of the screen, a slim rail of icons that is always there and opens to show each button's name, with its description on hover. Each person has their own profiles and buttons, colored by the kind of action. A button does one safe step or several in a row: open an Amit app already signed in, a website, a program or file, a menu (the Helper keeps one list of every menu and pop-up it can open), a Windows action (44 named actions such as Undo, Copy, Open Task View and Lock PC, released but not yet field-tested), play music, speak, or ask Amit. A button's icon can be picked from the list or be the person's own picture, imported in the Hub (a small picture kept on the computer where it was imported, so another computer shows a dot until it is imported there too). A Settings group always holds one standard, locked button, Amit menu, which opens the Amit menu and is what the middle mouse button runs. Every button can be pressed by voice, by saying its name, or by a mouse button. THE AURORA RING: the ring that opens when you hold the trigger mouse button (right by default) anywhere in Windows. By default it has five choices: Dictate (talk to type), Show Amit (take a picture of an area), Voice (say what to do), Read (read it aloud) and Mobile (a photo from your phone). The ring is the person's own: in the Aurora editor (a Helper window) they choose what sits on it (the five built-in choices, any button from their bar, or any menu the Helper can open, up to ten wedges), set the order, give each wedge a letter or their own drawing, keep several named sets and pick which set the ring shows. A set can also follow a whole bar profile, so the ring always shows exactly that profile's buttons. Each wedge shows its button's own icon (with seven or more wedges only icons are shown, larger, and the name appears in the middle on hover). The default set is an ordinary editable set that Reset to default puts back. Changes save at once and show the next time the ring opens; a button changed in the Hub reaches the ring in about ten seconds. The ring's centre Amit icon is Ask Amit and opens the Helper window, a small floating chat under the person's own sign-in; the first open each day is a morning wake-up, later opens are a small chat. Not yet tested by hand: the editor's buttons and the Hub's Import a picture button. THE AMIT MENU: one click of the middle mouse button (any mouse) opens it beside the pointer, with three tabs. Voice lists everything Voice understands (Voice, Dictate, built-in commands, the person's bar buttons and their own commands); choosing Voice turns listening on. Mouse recognizes which mouse opened the menu and lists that mouse's sets to scroll and pick, with an ON/OFF switch for all mouse sets and an Open button that goes to Amit Mouse in the Hub. Keyboard does the same for the keyboard last used. The wheel moves through the list, a click or the middle button chooses, Esc or a click elsewhere closes it. The menu and mouse keep working while dictation or Voice runs. The mouse and keyboard sets themselves are described on the Amit Mouse and Amit Keyboard cards. THE PHONE AS A PAD: a phone signed in to the person's Amit account, on the home Wi-Fi, becomes a touchpad and button pad for the computer. It opens to a home menu of Mouse, Navigation (Helper bar, Amit menu, Aurora and the person's own bar buttons), Photo and Ask Amit. At home, the Mouse and Buttons tile in Amit Mobile opens it. Each phone has its own name and appears in the Hub's Amit Phone tab, which lists phones, lets the person remove one and holds the pad's own on/off switch. The pad runs over plain http on the home network only. Not yet field-tested on a real phone: right click, scroll, pinch zoom, a second phone, Android. CUSTOM SCRIPT BUTTONS (new, first one built on 2026-11-24, tested on one computer): a button on the bar can run a small script that Amit writes for the person, with no Amit or Claude open when it is pressed. In the Hub (Helper tab, Custom script buttons) the person describes the job in their own words and any questions the button should ask them each time. There is no set number of questions: what the button has to do decides how many Amit asks while building it and how many the button asks when pressed. Where the ordinary button steps can do the whole job, Amit builds an ordinary button with no script. Otherwise Amit builds the script, and the Helper checks it against a never list (it may not delete files, change settings, reach the internet, read passwords or send anything by itself). A script may open secure websites through one approved tool (only the sites listed on the button's card or typed by the person, at most 10 a press), and a script that does so cannot read files, the clipboard or computer details. The person tries a practice run first, which shows exactly what it would do and changes nothing, then allows it to run for real; any change to the script asks for approval again. Pressing the button opens a small pop-up that asks its questions, shows the check screen, then runs, with a Stop button and a plain result card. Every file it changes is backed up first. For now building is limited to the owner, using their own Claude account; later each person builds with their own Claude account, and a person without one is kindly led to get one. Sending messages is locked until a mail connection exists. DICTATION, READ AND SHOW AMIT: Dictate types the person's words into the text box they are in and follows them to the next one; if they leave every text box while talking, the Dictate window opens by itself with the words and types them where they next click. Read reads aloud what the person points at (see the Read card). Show Amit is the screenshot and picture editor (see the Show Amit card). OTHER PARTS: hold-and-speak, the Amit Preview window, a welcome with real checks at every sign-in, and a record kept on the computer when an Amit program crashes. UPDATES: the Helper updates itself from the published list of files and never goes back to an older version. Needs the internet for Ask Amit and the natural voices; with no internet it says so plainly. Windows only. Still being designed, not built: switching a mouse's sets by voice, a scheduler for weekly script buttons, and an open chat window with a live preview for building a button by talking with Amit (today's Hub window asks six set questions first).

groups.title: Contracted work (jobs built for others, available for hire)

apps.name: NREMT Paramedic Study Guide
apps.desc: A free exam-prep tool for paramedic students preparing for the NREMT national exam, built end to end as a one-time job and live. It has 1,201 questions across five domains, flashcards, four practice modes (including practice by category and weak-spot review), two sealed final exams, timed exam simulations and a live scenario generator. Signed-in people get their progress and answer history saved to their account and synced, and pursuits can be scheduled in the Hub paced against their exam date; without sign-in it still works as a study tool. An Ask Amit button on the page lets a person ask why it is free. The content is deliberately plain and secular: it is a paramedic exam tool, not a tract; it is one of Amit's free tools whose generosity invites the question why. A companion page, How This Was Built, records the build timeline. It is a finished project with no open items. Available for hire: have a project? Write to Amit.

groups.title: Other applications we built (not part of Amit)

apps.name: Yamaha Recon Capture
apps.desc: A phone-friendly page built for one contracted business to simplify its monthly bookkeeping reconciliation. A person picks the month, then photographs the three source documents for that month: the daily point-of-sale reports, the merchant-services (card processor) statement and the bank statement. A Scan button on each also lets a scanner on the computer be used. Each photo is tagged with its month and uploaded to storage, and the same page shows a live viewer grouped by document type, with thumbnails, a click-to-enlarge view and a delete button, so the photos can be reviewed from the phone or the desktop. The page can be added to a phone's home screen. It is intake only: it does not read the figures or match anything automatically; the reconciliation itself is done afterward with Amit's help. It deliberately has no sign-in, so it is meant to be used only by the people given its address. It is separate from the Amit mission and not for general use.

apps.name: AeyeQ — Dog Race Analyzer
apps.desc: A greyhound race analysis tool built around Wheeling track programs. You enter a race (grade, distance and each dog's past performance lines, typed by hand or pasted and parsed with a checking step that lets you accept, re-paste or skip), and it scores every dog with a custom weighted rating built from form, class move, post, speed and break, with drill-down buttons (Break, Speed, Finish, Advance, Grade) showing what drives each score. Tabs: Race Entry, Scoring Config (adjust the weights), Race History, Performance Learn (compares predicted results to actual ones so the weights can be tuned), Bet Strategies, a Bet Calculator and Analytics. History, Learn, Strategies and Analytics are marked as premium features behind a sign-in; there is also an assistant button. It is an analysis aid only, with no real money handled. A plan to turn it into a virtual dog-racing game inside the Hub is recorded but not built. It opens from the Amit Games page.

planned.name: AskAmit
planned.desc: Not finished. A first version exists, and one thing is connected to it so far: the Hub's custom button builder for the Amit Helper, where Amit writes a person's own button (open to the owner only while it is being developed). AskAmit is meant to be the one shared Ask Amit module: a single home that answers people's questions, so the page buttons, the chat and Amit Mobile all use the same rules and abilities. A first build is running on its own: an answering engine, its database tables, a test page, and a chat-box door for visitors. It has three modes of answering (spiritual questions use Amit's full testimony, application questions use that application's own notes, general questions use a short companion standard) and a visitor rule (a few questions about the applications, then help signing up). Answers run on Amit's own Claude account for now; people who go Pro will connect their own. It is tested with real visitor answers and a measured cost, but the other Ask Amit doors (the page buttons, the chat and Amit Mobile) do not point to it yet.

planned.name: Amit Assembly
planned.desc: Designed, not built, and on the back burner by choice. A construction estimating, change-order, live-bidding and vendor-pricing platform, rebuilt from a roughly ten-year-old Access system (formerly called Bostonator). The core idea is a build-up of Items, Tasks, Assemblies and Packages, any layer open to bids. It would share client and vendor data with AmitBooks. The name is settled; no screens, tables or data exist yet.

planned.name: Amit Companion
planned.desc: Planned only. The idea is a discipleship companion with testimony tracking, daily encouragement and a deeper walk over time. No separate application exists; the Hub's daily features carry part of this for now.

planned.name: Amit Stewardship
planned.desc: A future concept only; nothing is built. The idea is to extend Computer Health's approach to the whole household: catalog the house, vehicle, appliances and tools, check their health, turn maintenance into Pursuits, and log when repairs are done. It is recorded on the to-do lists, under Computer Health.

planned.name: God Talk — The Ten Commandments
planned.desc: Planned as an interactive application. What exists today is a written study, not an app: one commandment at a time studied for its intent against the ESV, the KJV and the oldest Hebrew, tested honestly, with a hymn written alongside. Commandment 1 is fully organized as the template, Commandment 4 (Sabbath) has all six sections, and Commandments 2 and 3 have only discussion notes saved. Ryan's wider God Talk sessions now live in the GodTalk folder, one topic folder each (for example Exodus 24, Melchizedek, the new covenant promises), as notes, not as a public page.

planned.name: Amit Live
planned.desc: Amit's characters. A character is Amit as he works in one kind of work, such as writing a proposal or writing a devotion, with the rules for that work built in, so the care and the voice hold steady and no one has to keep repeating corrections. It is still one Amit, never a separate agent; each character points back to the testimony for what is true of Amit everywhere. Designed, not built.

planned.name: Computer Value
planned.desc: Designed, not built. The one-time paid diagnostic report for a person's computer, meant to bring in the income that keeps the rest of Amit free. The full spec is written and the first build stage is ready to begin, but only a draft placeholder page exists, not a finished report. Its free companion, Computer Health, is built and live separately.
